title: Lesya Ukrainka
summary: Lesya Ukrainka, born Larysa Petrivna Kosach on 25 February 1871, was a prominent Ukrainian writer known for her poetry and plays, as well as her activism for political, civil, and women's rights. Her works and life are deeply intertwined with the cultural and historical context of Ukraine.

sections.heading: Biography
paragraphs: Lesya Ukrainka was born in 1871 in Novohrad-Volynskyi, [[ukraine|Ukraine]]. She was the second child of Olha Drahomanova-Kosach, a [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] writer of Greek descent, and Petro Kosach, a head of the district assembly of conciliators from [[chernihiv|Chernihiv]] province. Her family was influential in the advancement of Ukrainian culture, with her father supporting Ukrainian publishing ventures.

Ukrainka completed her education at Chernihiv Gymnasium and was raised in a household where Ukrainian was the primary language. She learned to read at the age of four and was educated by Ukrainian tutors to avoid Russian-language schools.

sections.heading: Literary Career
paragraphs: Ukrainka began writing poetry at a young age, with her first poem, 'Hope,' written at eight years old. Her first published poem appeared in 1884, and she adopted her pseudonym to circumvent restrictions on Ukrainian language publications in the Russian Empire. Her first collection, 'On the Wings of Songs,' was published in 1893 in Western Ukraine and smuggled into [[kyiv|Kyiv]].

Throughout her career, Ukrainka produced significant works that reflected her belief in Ukraine's freedom. She was involved in the Literary and Artistic Society in Kyiv and founded a literary circle called Pleyada with her brother to promote [[ukrainian-literature|Ukrainian literature]].

sections.heading: Later Career and Activism
paragraphs: Ukrainka's health issues necessitated travel for better climates, leading her to various countries, including Germany, Italy, and Egypt. Her literary output included plays such as 'The Forest Song' and 'The Noblewoman,' which drew on Ukrainian history and folklore.

She was also politically active, opposing Russian tsarism and participating in Ukrainian Marxist organizations. In 1901, she translated 'The Communist Manifesto' into Ukrainian and faced arrest by the tsarist police in 1907.

sections.heading: Personal Life
paragraphs: Ukrainka's personal relationships, particularly with Olha Kobylianska, sparked considerable scholarly debate regarding her sexuality. Their correspondence included intimate expressions of affection, leading to the development of a gender-neutral language between them.
In 1897, she fell in love with Siarhej Miaržynski, who died in 1901. She later married Klyment Kvitka in 1907, and they lived in [[crimea|Crimea]] and Georgia.

sections.heading: Health and Legacy
paragraphs: Lesya Ukrainka suffered from bone tuberculosis, which was diagnosed in 1883 after years of misdiagnoses. Her health challenges influenced her literary themes and activism.
Ukrainka's contributions to Ukrainian literature and her role as an activist have solidified her legacy as a key figure in the cultural history of Ukraine.
